newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Glynwed cautious after H1 profit rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Glynwed cautious after H1 profit rise.

text.p: Industrial group Glynwed International Plc announced a 9.2 percent rise in headline profits for the half-year on Tuesday, but sounded a cautious note for the year.
The metals distribution to Aga cookers group reported pretax profits rose to 43.9 million pounds ($69.4 million) from 40.2 million pounds for the first six months of this year.
But chairman Gareth Davies said the British government's abolition of tax credits on dividend payments would result in an increase in the group's pension fund charge in the second half of the year.

He also warned that the strength of the pound could hit the year's result if recent exchange rates persisted, and the interim dividend was held at 4.4p a share, covered by earnings of 12.19 pence a share.

Underlying operating operating profits in the first six months rose 1.2 million pounds to 47.3 million pounds before exceptionals, on sales reduced by disposals to 632 million pounds, from 677.3 million a year ago.
The share price was down a 1/2p at 251-1/2p by 0838 GMT in a generally firmer market, having touched 249 earlier on disappointment that there was no increase in the interim dividend.
"I would have expected them to increase the dividend because for the year as a whole I see dividend cover of about two times," said Michael Blogg of Charterhouse Tilney.

"There was progress in margins in all four of the group's divisions," Blogg said. "But the strong warning on the impact of sterling will keep forecasts under control and we don't have any idea of the likely size of the pension charge."
Davies said it was too early to quantify the impact but warned that the effect on profits would "certainly outweigh" the benefits of the government's concurrent cut in corporation tax rates.

Davies also said the strength of the pound had made export conditions increasingly difficult in the first half and the overall impact of currency changes was estimated to have reduced first-half profits by about four million pounds.
If sterling's strength persisted Davies said it could offset further benefits from rationalisation efforts, but he went on to suggest that improved market conditions could still save the day.

"The impact of the strength of sterling will be offset if UK consumer spending remains strong, the increasingly important U.S. markets remain buoyant and continental Europe continues its gradual recovery," he said in his results statement.
"Against this complex background we remain cautiously optimistic about the out-turn for the year."
